result:
The constant is $c = 2/3$. The other agent's value of $1/2$ is ruled out by an explicit construction.

**Lower bound from a space barrier.** Let $S_i \subseteq V_i$ with $|S_i| = n/3$ for $i=1,2,3$, so $|S| = n-1$ in total. Let $H$ consist of all triples meeting $S$. Every edge meets $S$, so $H$ has no perfect matching, since a perfect matching would need $n$ pairwise disjoint edges, each using a vertex of $S$, but $|S| < n$.

Take $v \in V_1 \setminus S_1$. Its link is the bipartite graph between $V_2$ and $V_3$ whose edges meet $S_2 \cup S_3$, i.e. $K_{n,n}$ minus the complete bipartite graph on $(V_2\setminus S_2)\times(V_3\setminus S_3)$. Its biadjacency matrix, with blocks of relative sizes $1/3$ and $2/3$, has the reduced form

$$K=\begin{pmatrix}1/3 & \sqrt{2}/3\\ \sqrt{2}/3 & 0\end{pmatrix}\cdot n.$$

Its largest eigenvalue is $\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac13+1\right)n = \tfrac{2}{3}n$, so $\rho(N_H(v)) \approx \tfrac{2}{3}n$. By symmetry the same holds for vertices outside $S_2$ and $S_3$. Vertices in $S_i$ have links with spectral radius at least $n$ (their links contain $K_{n,n}$ minus at most a few edges... more precisely they can be given complete links without creating a perfect matching obstruction, so they do not lower the minimum). So every vertex has link spectral radius about $\tfrac{2}{3}n$, yet there is no perfect matching. Hence $c \ge 2/3$.

**Consistency check.** The minimum vertex degree of this construction is $(1-(2/3)^2)n = \tfrac{5}{9}n$, which matches the known minimum-vertex-degree threshold $5/9$ for perfect matchings in 3-partite 3-graphs. This supports the balanced cover as the extremal example. A spectral threshold of $2/3$ is consistent with it, since the spectral radius $\tfrac{2}{3}n$ exceeds the average link degree $\tfrac{5}{9}n$.

**Other candidate constructions.** Unbalanced covers give smaller minimum link radii. For example, $s_1 = 1/2$, $s_2 = s_3 = 1/4$ gives about $0.576n$ for the vertices outside $S_1$. I did not carry out a full optimality proof over all possible constructions, so the matching upper bound rests on the known result this problem refers to rather than on my own argument.

ANSWER: 2/3
